notes: Abuse-of-process appeal on successive RTA prosecutions; Elrington/Beedie principles and burden on Crown are clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: R v Phipps: abuse of process for dangerous driving after drink-driving conviction
key_facts: James Phipps drove the wrong way on the A3 at New Malden, collided head-on with another vehicle and recorded 50 microgrammes of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath.
He pleaded guilty in the magistrates' court to driving with excess alcohol and was fined and disqualified for twelve months.
After press and victim complaints the Crown summonsed him for dangerous driving arising from the same incident; he pleaded guilty following an unsuccessful abuse-of-process application.

The Crown Court judge held the dangerous-driving prosecution did not arise from the same or substantially the same facts as the drink-driving case because one concerned manner of driving and the other alcohol level.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence after guilty plea to dangerous driving, by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal against conviction allowed; the second prosecution should have been stayed as an abuse of process because both charges arose from the same incident and the Crown identified no special or exceptional circumstances.
enrichment.ratio: Subject to special or exceptional circumstances shown by the prosecution, a defendant must not be prosecuted again for a more serious offence arising out of the same or substantially the same facts after an earlier prosecution on the same incident has concluded; the burden is on the Crown, not the defence, and the question is not whether a fair trial remains possible.
legal_issues: Whether dangerous driving and drink driving on the same incident involve the same or substantially the same facts
Whether the Beedie/Ebrahim fair-trial abuse test applies to successive prosecutions
Whether special circumstances justified the second prosecution after magistrates' conviction
Interaction with Archbold guidance on order of trials for excess alcohol and dangerous driving

notes: Detailed Commercial Court trial of marine insurance preliminary issues; construction, rectification and estoppel rulings are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Thor Navigation v Ingosstrakh: valued or unvalued hull policies on THOR II
key_facts: Thor Navigation insured the vessel THOR II under fleet hull policies with Ingosstrakh (40%) and SOVAG (60%) listing a sum insured of US$1.5m but no agreed value wording.
After shaft and engine damage at Piraeus in September 2002 the owners claimed constructive total loss; insurers declined abandonment and said repairs would cost less than the sum insured.
Owners contended the policies were valued, or alternatively that insurers were estopped or the policies should be rectified because brokers had requested valued cover.
Insurers consistently quoted and issued policies using 'SUM INSURED' only, reflecting their deliberate preference for unvalued Russian-market terms.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on policy construction, estoppel, rectification and measure of insurable value after case management by Cresswell J.
enrichment.outcome: Policies held unvalued on construction; rectification and estoppel claims failed; on an unvalued policy the insurable value for a constructive total loss is the market value at time and place of loss ($800,000), not the section 16(1) formula.
enrichment.ratio: The term 'sum insured' without words of valuation ordinarily denotes an unvalued marine policy setting a ceiling on recovery, even where Institute Time Clauses refer to insured value; market practice and ITCH incorporation cannot override clear wording, and rectification or estoppel requires shared or dishonestly known mistake which was not established.
legal_issues: Whether 'sum insured' in fleet policies specified an agreed value under section 27(2)
Whether incorporation of ITCH clauses made the policies valued by English market practice
Whether common or unilateral mistake entitled owners to rectification
Whether insurers were estopped from denying valued cover
Correct measure of indemnity on an unvalued hull policy under section 68 and ITCH clause 6

notes: Section 67 rehearing on arbitral jurisdiction; narrow construction of LME counterclaim scope is carefully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Metal Distributors v ZCCM: LME tribunal jurisdiction over debt-rescheduling counterclaim
key_facts: MDL owed ZCCM $3,036,396.79 under a May 2000 compromise settling copper and cobalt sales contracts containing LME arbitration clauses.
MDL counterclaimed for $1.5m lent to Ramcoz, alleging ZCCM misrepresented or collaterally agreed to comply with an alleged debt rescheduling proposal.
ZCCM denied any concluded debt rescheduling agreement and argued the counterclaim was unrelated to the sales contracts.
An LME tribunal ruled it had no jurisdiction over the counterclaim; MDL challenged that ruling under section 67.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 67 application to set aside a preliminary arbitral award on jurisdiction, heard de novo by Cresswell J.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the tribunal correctly held it had no jurisdiction because the counterclaim concerned an independent alleged collateral contract and misrepresentation about debt restructuring, not disputes under the sales contracts.
enrichment.ratio: Arbitral jurisdiction depends on party consent and the true construction of the arbitration agreement; unlike courts, tribunals cannot entertain independent set-offs or counterclaims outside the scope of the agreed clause, and LME Rule 6 counterclaims are not co-extensive with court counterclaim jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Scope of counterclaims under LME Arbitration Rule 6
Whether independent set-off principles from Aectra apply in arbitration
Construction of clauses referring to disputes 'under this contract'
Whether alleged debt rescheduling representations fell within sales-contract arbitration clauses

notes: Urgent construction of CJA 2003 s.141 transitional scope; Vice President's reasoning addresses practical consequences in detail.

enrichment.short_title: R v Bradley: when CJA 2003 Part 11 bad character provisions apply
key_facts: Bradley was charged in July 2004 with robbery and possessing an imitation firearm but his trial began on 15 December 2004, the commencement date for Part 11 bad character provisions.
The judge admitted evidence of his 2000 robbery conviction under section 101(1)(d) as relevant to an important matter in issue.
Bradley appealed on the ground that Part 11 could not apply because criminal proceedings had begun before 15 December when he was charged.
The Crown contended the new rules applied because the trial itself began on or after commencement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent certified appeal against conviction on the transitional commencement of Part 11 evidence provisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Part 11 applies to all trials and Newton hearings begun on or after commencement, even if the defendant was charged earlier; the previous robbery conviction was admissible.
enrichment.ratio: 'Criminal proceedings' in section 141 bears the same meaning as in sections 112(1), 134(1) and 140—proceedings in relation to which the strict rules of evidence apply, namely trials and Newton hearings—so the transitional provision prevents mid-hearing rule changes but not application to pending cases whose trials start after commencement.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'criminal proceedings begun' in section 141
Whether Part 11 applies by charge date or trial start date
Interaction with Crown Court bad character notice rules
Practical consequences for joint trials and mixed-charge defendants

notes: Commercial Court summary judgment on FOB crude oil payment terms; no set-off clause analysis is detailed and well supported.

enrichment.short_title: Totsa v Bharat Petroleum: no set-off clause bars water-in-cargo price defence
key_facts: Totsa sold Forcados crude FOB Nigeria to Bharat Petroleum; payment was due 30 days after bill of lading without discount, deduction, set-off or counterclaim.
Bharat issued an irrevocable payment undertaking to pay the full invoice without set-off, deduction or counterclaim.
Shore-tank measurements on the bills of lading showed 949,092 barrels invoiced at $38.915 per barrel, but Bharat paid only part of the price claiming up to 45,000 barrels were water.
Clause IX of the Elf 90 general terms required shore-tank quantities to be used for invoicing after deduction of BS&W.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Summary judgment application in the Commercial Court on whether buyers could withhold part of the contract price.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for the sellers; the restrictive payment and undertaking clauses precluded the buyers from paying less than the invoiced amount and required any shortage claim to be pursued separately.
enrichment.ratio: Where an FOB oil contract and payment undertaking prohibit deduction, withholding, set-off and counterclaim, a buyer who refuses to pay the full invoice because part of the cargo was water rather than oil is seeking to deduct or withhold payment and cannot rely on a 'pure defence' or abatement to avoid the clause; Mondel v Steel-type defences are excluded by clear words.
legal_issues: Whether a shortage-of-oil defence is a pure defence or a deduction barred by contract
Construction of no set-off and no withholding clauses in commodity sales
Effect of shore-tank measurement clauses on invoicing rights
Whether abatement under section 53(1) survives express contractual exclusion

notes: Extended licence appeal in intra-familial sexual abuse case; Nelson principles on extension period applied.

enrichment.short_title: R v GB: extended licence for indecent assault and anal rape of nieces
key_facts: GB, aged 31, was convicted of five indecent assaults and anal rape of his young nieces K and S over nearly a decade in a family where his father and cousin were also convicted of serious sexual offences.
He received concurrent sentences including nine years for anal rape of S aged 12, plus a six-year extension period under section 85, totalling 13 years custody and seven years extension.
Psychiatric evidence found no mental illness but identified high reoffending risk to known children while he denied the offences.
The sentencing judge treated anal rape of a 12-year-old as especially grave though not inherently longer than vaginal rape.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the single judge, focusing on totality and the section 85 extension period.
enrichment.outcome: Custodial terms upheld as not manifestly excessive; appeal allowed only to set aside the six-year extension period on count 45, leaving 13 years' imprisonment in total.
enrichment.ratio: An extended licence period under section 85 is a public-protection measure distinct from reflecting offence seriousness; where a substantial custodial term already carries a lengthy ordinary licence, an additional extension of six years may be disproportionate, especially where risk is confined to family settings and standard licence supervision will apply.
legal_issues: Whether nine years for anal rape of a 12-year-old niece was manifestly excessive
Appropriate totality where concurrent indecent assault sentences were imposed
Justification and length of a section 85 extension where the offender denied guilt
Whether anal and vaginal rape attract different starting points

notes: Fresh evidence appeal on trust and loan dispute; Ladd v Marshall analysis and retrial order are clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Nicolet v Halim: retrial after newly discovered letters on flat trust
key_facts: Accountant Mr Nicolet bought a Gerrards Cross flat in his name in 1999; Miss Halim occupied it and claimed he held it on trust for her absolutely.
The county court judge preferred Nicolet's account that she had only a licence to renovate and share proceeds, and found a £225,076 loan was repayable.
After judgment Halim discovered handwritten letters from Nicolet in 1999 describing himself as nominee/trustee and agreeing to transfer the property at cost.
The letters contradicted trial evidence and could not be explained as documents prepared for third parties like earlier 1999 formal papers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Oxford County Court possession and money judgment; court first decided whether to admit fresh evidence under Ladd v Marshall.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment set aside and re-trial ordered before a different judge at Central London County Court on both the flat ownership and money claims.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh evidence discovered after trial may be admitted on appeal where it could not reasonably have been obtained earlier, would probably have had an important influence on the result, and is apparently credible; where such documents undermine a credibility-based judgment, justice requires a re-trial even though the first judge's findings were otherwise sound.
legal_issues: Whether newly discovered 1999 letters satisfied Ladd v Marshall criteria
Effect of fresh evidence on credibility findings as to beneficial ownership
Whether the money claim should be retried with the property dispute
Distinction between documents created for third parties and personal correspondence

enrichment.short_title: Council for National Parks v Pembrokeshire: no costs after Bluestone JR loss
key_facts: The Council for National Parks unsuccessfully challenged the Bluestone planning decision granted by the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park Authority.
The Council had no private interest, limited resources, and brought the claim as a public interest challenge to a decision of public importance.
The developers sought costs as interested parties; the Park Authority ordinarily would recover costs on failure.
The Council sought permission to appeal on whether local economic benefit could override policy GE4's overriding national need requirement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs applications and permission to appeal following substantive judicial review judgment dismissing the planning challenge.
enrichment.outcome: No order that the Council pay the Park Authority's or developers' costs; permission to appeal refused on the section 54A/GE4 economic benefit point.
enrichment.ratio: A public interest environmental claimant without private stake may be spared the usual costs-follow-the-event order where the challenge concerned a matter of public importance; developers do not recover a second set of costs unless they had a separate interest requiring separate arguments, and local economic benefit is a material planning consideration that does not require an overriding national need equivalent to Green Belt policy.
legal_issues: Whether a public interest challenger should pay costs after losing a planning JR
Whether developers had a separate interest entitling them to costs under Bolton MDC principles
Whether Pembrokeshire economic benefit could justify departure from policy GE4
Applicability of Buckland/Smith Green Belt reasoning outside the Green Belt

enrichment.short_title: R (SC) v MHRT: restricted patient section 75 discharge and classified disorder
key_facts: SC received a section 37 hospital order with indefinite section 41 restrictions after conviction for GBH with intent, classified as suffering from mental illness.
Conditionally discharged in June 2001, he applied under section 75(2) for the restriction order to cease so he would no longer be liable to recall.
The Tribunal refused absolute discharge, varied conditions, and relied on past psychopathic personality assessments despite mental illness being the only classified disorder.
SC argued the Tribunal unlawfully considered unclassified personality disorder and that section 75(3) lacked sufficient criteria to comply with Articles 6 and 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Mental Health Review Tribunal decision refusing to direct that a restriction order cease to have effect.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Tribunal lawfully considered non-classified disorders when exercising section 75(3) discretion, and section 75(3) is compatible with the Convention given statutory context and procedural safeguards.
enrichment.ratio: The R(B) v Ashworth theme linking detention to classified disorder does not prevent a Tribunal from considering other mental health history when deciding under section 75(3) whether a restriction order should cease; section 73 shows conditional discharge may remain appropriate even without current classified disorder, and section 75(3) is sufficiently foreseeable when read with sections 37, 41 and 73 plus judicial review and Tribunal procedure.
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal may rely on unclassified psychopathic disorder in a section 75 application
Application of R(B) v Ashworth to restriction order discharge decisions
Whether section 75(3) satisfies Article 6 and Article 8 foreseeability requirements
Proper criteria when section 73 does not apply to section 75(2) applications

notes: Low-velocity impact appeal; expert vs witness-of-fact guidance from Cooper Payen applied and distinguished.

enrichment.short_title: Armstrong v First York: low-velocity impact and single joint expert evidence
key_facts: Mr Armstrong and Miss Connor claimed soft tissue spine injuries after a bus glanced their stationary Ford Fiesta at a York junction, causing minor paint damage.
Single joint expert Mr Childs concluded occupant displacement sufficient to cause injury was impossible without panel distortion or vehicle movement on the road.
The trial judge found the claimants honest and credible, rejected fraud, and preferred their evidence of a jolt over the expert reconstruction.
The defendant had pleaded fraud in the alternative and allocated the case to the multi-track.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Liverpool County Court liability judgment after agreed damages; permission granted because similar low-velocity impact cases were pending.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge lawfully chose claimant witness evidence over the single joint expert where he could not identify a technical flaw but was not satisfied the claim was fraudulent.
enrichment.ratio: There is no rule that single joint expert evidence on occupant displacement in low-velocity impacts must be dispositive; where direct witness evidence conflicts with expert reconstruction, the trial judge may prefer credible witnesses of fact without pinpointing technical error in the expert, especially where rejecting the expert would imply fraud not established on the evidence.
legal_issues: Weight to be given to single joint expert evidence against witnesses of fact
Whether a judge must identify specific error before rejecting expert evidence
Application of Cooper Payen and Flannery principles to low-velocity whiplash claims
Whether preferring claimants necessarily required a finding of fraud
